title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A plain German statement comes out in the order you already think in: subject, then verb, then the rest. Ich wohne in Berlin is "I live in Berlin", word for word.

You give your name with ich heiße — heißen is "to be called", so it is literally "I am called Anna". Take the two words as one chunk; the person lives in the ending, ich heiße for yourself and Sie heißen for whoever you are speaking to.

sein is the one verb "to be" and it is irregular, so it is learned rather than built: ich bin · er/sie/es ist · Sie sind. That single verb does every job English's "be" does — who you are, what state you are in, and where a thing is. There is no second "to be" to choose between.

A regular verb marks the person in its ending: -e for ich, -en for Sie. ich komme · Sie kommen, ich wohne · Sie wohnen. The -en form is spelled exactly like the infinitive, so learning one shape gives you both.

This course speaks Sie — the form you use with a shopkeeper, a landlord, an official or a colleague, where it is never wrong. German also has a familiar du with a whole second set of endings; choosing it is a later level's job, so nothing in this course is written with it.

Every German noun has one of three genders and its article shows which: der (m) · die (f) · das (n). Learn each noun WITH its article. The ending is often a real clue — a noun in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion or -tät is feminine, one in -chen or -lein is neuter, an -er agent noun like Lehrer is masculine — and what is left over is genuinely learned rather than guessed.

Every noun is written with a CAPITAL letter, anywhere in the sentence: der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch, Ich mag Kaffee. This is not emphasis and it is not optional — the capital is how German marks a noun, and you have to produce it every time.
ein (m and n) and eine (f) are the German "a", and they follow the same three-way gender as der/die/das: ein Tisch, eine Tür, ein Buch.
English puts "a" in front of a job and German leaves it out: Ich bin Student, never Ich bin ein Student. The article comes back only once something describes the noun.

A whole CLASS of thing takes a bare noun: Ich mag Kaffee is "I like coffee". Put der in front and you have narrowed it to one particular cup — Ich mag den Kaffee is "I like this coffee here". This is the opposite of French and Spanish, which use the definite article for the class (J'aime le café, Me gusta el café), so a habit from either language will mislead you here as surely as the English one.
German writes the subject pronoun every time, exactly as English does: ich is never dropped.

das does two jobs. In front of a neuter noun it is "the": das Buch. Standing alone in front of ist it points at something — Das ist der Tisch, "that is the table" — and it points at anything at all, whatever gender the thing turns out to have.

The umlaut and the ß are letters, not decorations. Tür is not spelled with a bare u, and heiße is not spelled with a double s: change either one and you have written a different word, or no word at all.

words.cue: my name is · I am called
words.note: heißen, “to be called” — how a name is given. Take the two words as one chunk; the person lives in the ending: ich heiße, Sie heißen. The ß spells a long vowel; never write ss here.
A woman's name. Names carry over unchanged — swap in your own. They take a capital in German exactly as in English, and so, unlike English, does every other noun.

sentences.trap: Mein Name ist Anna is the English sentence translated word for word. It is grammatical, and it is stiff — a form you fill in rather than a person you meet. Ich heiße Anna is what is actually said.
sentences.sound: Three chunks: ish HIGH-suh AH-nah. The ch of ich is a soft hiss made at the front of the mouth, never a k. ei is always "eye", so heiße rhymes with English "nicer" minus the r, and the ß in the middle is a plain sharp s, never a z. The final -e of heiße is a real, unstressed "uh" — German never leaves a final -e silent the way French does.

variations.changed: swap the name — ich heiße itself never moves
the person shifts to the one you are speaking to, and the ending goes from -e to -en
a different verb does the same job — a name can follow ich bin, which is shorter and a little more casual

mistake.why: There is no second verb. heiße is already the verb of this sentence — English "my name IS" is what pushes an ist in, and German has no room for it.

sentences.usage: The first line of any introduction, to anyone at all.
sentences.mnemonic: heißen is "to be called". You are not saying what your name is, you are saying what you are called — so ich heiße, and nothing else.

words.note: I. German always writes the subject pronoun, as English does — but lowercase mid-sentence: capitals are for nouns, and for Sie.
kommen, “to come”. The ending names the person: ich komme, Sie kommen — and Sie kommen is spelled like the infinitive, which is why this course speaks Sie.
aus is the “from” of ORIGIN — Ich komme aus Indien. English has one “from”; German splits it, and a person or point you left takes a different word. Later, aus is also “out of”.
India. Country and town names carry over, capital and all, and most of them take no article at all: aus Indien, in Indien.

sentences.trap: English says "I am from India" with the verb "to be". German says it with "come": Ich komme aus Indien. Ich bin aus Indien exists and sounds like a translation; the ordinary sentence uses kommen.
sentences.sound: ish KOM-uh owss IN-dee-en. The final -e of komme is a genuine unstressed "uh", never silent. aus rhymes with English "house". Indien is three syllables with the stress on the first, and its d is a clean d, not the American flapped one.

variations.changed: swap the place — the frame Ich komme aus … is what stays
the person shifts to Sie, and the verb ending goes -e → -en
a name takes the subject slot, and sein replaces kommen — the same fact stated the flatter way

mistake.why: von is the "from" of a person or of a point you moved away from. An origin — the country or town you come from — takes aus.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second line of any introduction, and the one a stranger will actually ask about.
sentences.mnemonic: You come OUT of the place you are from: aus, which is the same aus as "out".

words.note: wohnen, “to live” at an address: ich wohne, Sie wohnen. German has another verb for being alive; an address always wants wohnen.
in, as in English: in Berlin, in Indien — a place name takes no article. Later, inside a thing, the ARTICLE after in changes (im Park vs in den Park); in itself never does.
Berlin. Town names carry over unchanged and take no article: in Berlin, aus Berlin. The stress is on the second syllable in German, as it is in English.

sentences.trap: "Live" is one English word covering two German ones. wohnen is where your address is; the other is being alive. Reach for the wrong one and the sentence still parses — it just stops being about Berlin.
sentences.sound: ish VOH-nuh in bair-LEEN. German w is an English v, every time: wohne begins with a v sound. The oh is long and pure, with no glide sliding off the end of it. The r of Berlin is made far back in the throat and barely sounds at all.

variations.changed: swap the place — a country works in the same frame as a town
the person shifts to Sie and the ending goes -e → -en, exactly as it did on kommen
wohnen → kommen: where you live against where you are from. Berlin can be both, one, or neither

mistake.why: A town or country name takes no article: in Berlin, in Indien, aus Indien. The article belongs to ordinary nouns, not to place names.

sentences.usage: Where you live now — said at a counter, on a form read aloud, or to anyone who has just asked where you are from.
sentences.mnemonic: wohnen and English "won" share a sound but not a meaning; think of a place you have WON and settled into.

words.note: sein, “to be” — irregular, so learned whole: ich bin · er/sie/es ist · Sie sind. One verb for every English “be”: who you are, how you feel, where a thing is.
A student — der Student, die Studentin. Every noun takes a capital; -in makes an agent noun feminine (Lehrer/Lehrerin). After sein a job stands bare: Ich bin Student.

sentences.trap: English cannot say "I am student" — it needs "a". German cannot say Ich bin ein Student for a plain job. The article you have spent your life inserting is exactly the one German wants left out, and it comes back only once something describes the noun.
sentences.sound: ish bin shtoo-DENT. An initial st- is "sht" in German, always — Student, Straße, Stuhl. The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -t is crisp. bin is short, like the English word.

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: the -in ending marks a woman: Student → Studentin, and the article behind it would be die, not der
a name takes the subject slot, and bin becomes ist for a third person
the person shifts to Sie, and sein's form for it is sind — the same shape as the they-form

mistake.why: No ein in front of a bare job after sein. It returns only once something describes the noun — Ich bin ein guter Student — which is a later rung's sentence.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do: a job, a course of study, a role. The same bare shape works for Ich bin Lehrer, Ich bin Kellner.
sentences.mnemonic: A job after sein stands on its own two feet: bin Student, not bin ein Student.

words.note: mögen, “to like” as a standing preference. mag takes no ending for ich or er/sie/es: ich mag, Anna mag. Ich möchte (“I would like”) is a different word — a later rung.
Coffee — der Kaffee, capitalised. A class of thing takes a BARE noun: Ich mag Kaffee. English agrees; French and Spanish add the article, and Ich mag den Kaffee means one particular cup.

sentences.trap: The trap here is not English, it is any Romance language you have met. French and Spanish say "I like THE coffee" for coffee in general; German, like English, says it bare.
sentences.sound: ish mahk KAH-fay. A final g hardens to a k, so mag ends in the sound of "mock". Kaffee is stressed on the FIRST syllable, unlike English "café", and both e's at the end run together into one long "ay".

variations.changed: swap what is liked — a place needs no article either
the person shifts to a third person and mag does not move — no -s, no ending, nothing
an article appears, and the meaning narrows: not books in general but this one book

mistake.why: Grammatical German, and not this sentence. With the article it means one particular coffee — the cup in front of you. Coffee as a class of thing goes bare: Ich mag Kaffee.

sentences.usage: Standing preferences — food, drink, places, music. For ordering something at a counter, a later rung gives you the polite Ich möchte.
sentences.mnemonic: mag is one syllable and takes no ending in any person you will use — the laziest verb in the rung.

words.note: Two jobs: “the” before a neuter noun (das Buch), or POINTING before ist — Das ist der Tisch — where it ignores the thing's gender: Das ist die Tür is right too.
“The” for a masculine noun: der Tisch, der Kaffee. Three articles where English has one — learn every noun WITH its article. der also appears before a feminine noun after some prepositions.
Table — masculine: der Tisch. Nothing in the word says so; this is one of the ones that is genuinely learned rather than worked out. Capital T, wherever it stands in the sentence.

sentences.trap: English has one "the" and never has to think about it. German has three, and the one you pick is fixed by the noun, not by the sentence: der Tisch is der whatever else happens around it.
sentences.sound: dass ist dair TISH. der is "dair" with a throaty r that fades almost to a vowel — closer to "deh-uh" than to English "dare". -sch is always the sh of "fish", so Tisch rhymes with it.

variations.changed: a different masculine noun — der does not move, because the noun is still masculine
the article-and-noun becomes the subject, and sein now says where something is rather than what it is
der → ein: the one we both mean becomes any one at all

mistake.why: A single countable noun does not stand bare here — it needs its article: der Tisch. The bare noun is for a whole class after mögen (Ich mag Kaffee) and for a job after sein (Ich bin Student), and this is neither.

sentences.usage: Pointing something out — in a room, in a shop, on a page.
sentences.mnemonic: Das ist … is the pointing finger of German, and it never changes shape no matter what it points at.

words.note: “The” for a feminine noun (die Tür) — and for the plural of every gender (die Tische, die Bücher). Which one it is, the noun's shape tells you.
Door — die Tür. The ü is a letter, not decoration: schon and schön are different words. Write the dots every time.

sentences.trap: Nothing about a door is female, and nothing about a table is male. Gender in German is a property of the WORD, not of the thing — which is why the article has to be learned with the noun instead of reasoned out from the world.
sentences.sound: dass ist dee tür. die is "dee" — ie is read by its second letter, and it is nothing like the English word spelled the same way. ü has no English twin: say "ee" and round your lips as though for "oo" without moving your tongue. Tür comes out roughly as "tewr".

variations.changed: a different feminine noun — die holds, because Studentin is feminine too
the article-and-noun moves into the subject slot and sein says where she is
die → eine: the door we both mean becomes any door at all

mistake.why: Tür is feminine, so its article is die. der in front of a noun like this makes it masculine, which Tür is not.

sentences.usage: Pointing at a thing and naming it — the sentence a shop assistant or a landlord will use on you constantly.
sentences.mnemonic: die and Tür both carry a long thin vowel; pair the sound of the article with the sound of the noun and the gender travels with it.

words.note: Book — das Buch. Neuter is the third box English has no twin for and the gender most often guessed wrong; learn das Buch as one piece.

sentences.trap: This line writes das twice and means something different each time: the first points ("that"), the second is the article of a neuter noun ("the"). One word, two jobs, and only the position tells you which is which.
sentences.sound: dass ist dass BOOKH. Buch has a long u, and the ch after it is the rasping sound at the back of the throat you hear in Scottish "loch" — a different sound from the soft ch of ich, and which one you get depends on the vowel in front of it.

variations.changed: the same das, now doing only the article job after mögen — and the meaning narrows to this one book
the article-and-noun becomes the subject and sein locates it
das → ein: the neuter "a" is spelled the same as the masculine one

mistake.why: Buch is neuter, so its article is das. die would make it feminine — and neuter is exactly the box an English speaker forgets exists.

sentences.usage: Pointing at a thing and naming it; and the first place you will see das doing both of its jobs in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: Das ist das … — when the pointing word and the article match, the noun is neuter.

words.note: “A” before a masculine OR neuter noun: ein Tisch, ein Buch. Feminine takes eine. No plural, as English has none — and it drops before a bare job after sein: Ich bin Student.

sentences.trap: ein and eine look like a small spelling difference and they are not: they are the masculine-and-neuter shape against the feminine one, and the noun decides which you write.
sentences.sound: dass ist eyn TISH. ei is always "eye", so ein rhymes with English "nine". Set it beside die from the last card: ei is read by its second letter and so is ie, which is why ein is "eyn" and die is "dee".

variations.changed: another masculine noun in the same slot — ein holds
ein → der: any table at all becomes the one we both mean
the ein-phrase takes the subject slot, and sein says where he is

mistake.why: eine is the feminine shape. Tisch is masculine, so it takes ein — the ending on eine is what marks the feminine, and adding it to a masculine noun is the commonest slip in this rung.

sentences.usage: Naming something for the first time, when neither of you has it in mind yet. Once you both do, it becomes der Tisch.
sentences.mnemonic: ein is one syllable for two genders; eine has one syllable more for the one gender left.

words.note: “A” before a feminine noun: eine Tür. The -e is the feminine mark you hear in die. Later, masculine ein grows an ending as an object; eine and neuter ein never change.

sentences.trap: Two of the three genders share ein and only one has eine — so the odds are against the ending, and English gives you no reason to add it. Anchor it to the noun: Tür is feminine, therefore eine Tür.
sentences.sound: dass ist EYE-nuh tür. eine is two syllables where ein is one: that final -e is an audible unstressed "uh", so the feminine article is genuinely longer in the mouth, not only on the page.

variations.changed: another feminine noun — the -in ending on the noun and the -e on the article agree
the eine-phrase takes the subject slot and sein says where she is
eine → die: any door at all becomes the one we both mean

mistake.why: Tür is feminine and takes eine. Bare ein would make it masculine or neuter — and dropping the -e is exactly what an English ear, which hears no difference worth keeping, will do.

sentences.usage: Naming a feminine thing for the first time. The pair to hold in your head is ein Tisch / eine Tür.
sentences.mnemonic: The feminine article is the longer one in both rows: die is longer than der in the mouth, and eine is longer than ein on the page.

comprehensionPool.cue: Anna is a student in Berlin
